title: Indian Markets Log Worst Week in Four Months as Brent Crude Surges Past $100
excerpt: Escalating Middle East tensions and soaring oil prices trigger a fifth straight session of losses, with the Sensex shedding over 3% in a week that rattled investor confidence across sectors.
body:
• The Sensex and Nifty are set for their worst weekly performance in four months, dropping 3.1% and 2.7% respectively over five consecutive losing sessions.
  • Brent crude surged past $100 per barrel after U.S. President Trump threatened military action against Iran and Houthi allies following Red Sea tanker strikes.
  • Fifteen of 16 major sectors logged losses, with oil marketing companies, IT bellwether Infosys and airline operator IndiGo among the hardest hit.
  • Foreign institutional investors continued selling Indian equities, adding to sustained downward pressure on benchmarks.

Fifth Straight Day of Losses

Indian equity markets extended their punishing sell-off on Friday, with benchmark indices sliding for a fifth consecutive session as Brent crude oil breached the $100-per-barrel mark amid escalating Middle East hostilities.

The BSE Sensex fell 0.91% to 75,700.9, while the Nifty 50 dropped 0.8% to 23,678 in early trade, according to Reuters. For the week, the benchmarks have shed approximately 3.1% and 2.7% respectively — their steepest weekly decline in four months.

The slide followed Thursday's session, where the Sensex had already dropped 363.66 points to close at 76,391.39, and the Nifty 50 fell 126.65 points to settle at 23,869.60, according to Outlook Business.

Oil Spike Fueled by Middle East Escalation

The immediate trigger was a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions. U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday promised "major military punishment" for Iran and its Houthi allies after Yemeni fighters struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, extending the conflict to a second major shipping chokepoint, Reuters reported.

Brent crude has now climbed above $100 per barrel, raising alarm bells for India — the world's third-largest crude oil importer and consumer. Higher oil prices threaten to stoke inflation, widen the country's trade deficit, and squeeze both economic growth and corporate profit margins.

"The concerns over Mideast tensions have been further amplified this week by a sharp rise in crude oil prices, hurting investor sentiment."

— Sunny Agrawal, Head of Fundamental Research, SBI Securities

"Broader markets also remain under pressure, reflecting cautious risk appetite among investors, with developments around the U.S.-Iran conflict and oil price movements likely driving market direction in the near term," Agrawal added.

Broad-Based Selling Across Sectors

The damage was widespread. Fifteen of the 16 major sectoral indices logged losses on Friday, with small-caps and mid-caps each falling 0.8%.

Oil marketing companies bore the brunt of the crude surge, with Bharat Petroleum (BPCL), Hindustan Petroleum (HPCL) and Indian Oil Corporation each dropping approximately 2%. These companies face a direct margin squeeze as input costs rise while retail fuel prices remain politically sensitive.

Weak June-quarter earnings compounded the pain. IT bellwether Infosys fell roughly 1.7% after reporting subdued results, while InterGlobe Aviation — India's largest airline and acutely exposed to jet fuel costs — shed about 2.4% on disappointing quarterly numbers.

On Thursday, the sell-off was led by Adani Enterprises, Shriram Finance, Nestle India, Adani Ports and Bajaj Finance, according to Outlook Business. Auto stocks were a rare bright spot, with Bajaj Auto, Mahindra & Mahindra and Eicher Motors bucking the trend on the back of strong earnings.

Market breadth underscored the bearish mood: on Thursday alone, 2,479 stocks declined against just 1,569 advancing on the NSE.

What This Means for NRI Investors

For the Indian diaspora with exposure to domestic equities, the sell-off presents both risks and potential opportunities. A sustained crude price above $100 could weaken the rupee further, eroding returns for NRI investors when converted to dollars or other foreign currencies. Foreign institutional investors have continued to pull money out of Indian markets, a trend that has persisted through much of 2026.

However, the sharp correction has also brought valuations closer to levels that attracted domestic buying during previous dips. Investors with a longer time horizon may find selective opportunities in sectors less exposed to oil prices, such as pharmaceuticals and healthcare.

Oil Trajectory to Drive Near-Term Direction

The trajectory of Brent crude and the evolving Middle East situation will be the dominant factors for Indian markets in the coming sessions. Any further escalation — particularly disruptions to oil supply routes through the Strait of Hormuz — could deepen losses, while signs of diplomatic progress may provide relief.

Earnings season is also in full swing, and upcoming results from major financial and industrial companies will test whether corporate India can weather the oil shock. With 15 of 16 sectors in the red and foreign investors heading for the exits, the burden of supporting the market falls increasingly on domestic institutional buyers.
nri_angle: Rising oil prices threaten to weaken the rupee, eroding returns for NRI equity investors. Continued FII selling and macroeconomic headwinds from crude imports may reshape portfolio allocations for diaspora investors with Indian market exposure.
author: Diaspora Desk
